The first 72 h following aneurysm rupture play a key role in determining clinical and cognitive outcomes after subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). Yet, very little is known about the impact of so called “early brain injury” on patents with clinically good grade SAH (as defined as World Federation of Neurosurgeons Grade 1 and 2). 27 patients with good grade SAH underwent MRI scanning were prospectively recruited at three time-points after SAH: within the first 72 h (acute phase), at 5–10 days and at 3 months. Patients underwent additional, comprehensive cognitive assessment 3 months post-SAH. 27 paired healthy controls were also recruited for comparison. In the first 72 h post-SAH, patients had significantly higher global and regional brain volume than controls. This change was accompanied by restricted water diffusion in patients. Persisting abnormalities in the volume of the posterior cerebellum at 3 months post-SAH were present to those patients with worse cognitive outcome. When using this residual abnormal brain area as a region of interest in the acute-phase scans, we could predict with an accuracy of 84% (sensitivity 82%, specificity 86%) which patients would develop cognitive impairment 3 months later, despite initially appearing clinically indistinguishable from those making full recovery. In an exploratory sample of good clinical grade SAH patients compared to healthy controls, we identified a region of the posterior cerebellum for which acute changes on MRI were associated with cognitive impairment. Whilst further investigation will be required to confirm causality, use of this finding as a risk stratification biomarker is promising. Wellcome Trust 203139/Z/16/Z issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2021 Introduction Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is a devastating disease with high mortality and morbidity in those patients who survive hospital treatment. Despite accounting for only 5% of all strokes, the socioeconomic cost of SAH has remained disproportionately high with a loss of functional years equivalent to ischaemic stroke. This is because despite reductions in the incidence of SAH 1 , 2 and mortality 3 , the disease often affects young adults of working age and frequently results in poor neurocognitive outcome 4 . Following successful aneurysm treatment, the management of patients with SAH is conventionally focused on the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of secondary brain injury caused by delayed cerebral ischaemia 5 . However, there is increasing evidence that damage caused in the first 72 h post-rupture—so called “early brain injury”—may play a key role not only in the development of such delayed cerebral ischaemia, but also in determining overall neurocognitive outcomes 6 . Early cerebral ischemia and infarction is common in the acute period after SAH and is associated with worse neurological and physiological admission status, as well as poor neurocognitive outcomes 7 , 8 . Global cerebral oedema is also a significant feature of early brain injury and is an independent risk factor for mortality and poor outcome after SAH 9 , 10 . Advances in MRI physics and analysis now offer a number of objective, reliable and non-invasive tools such as apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) and voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to measure changes in cerebral structure at a tissue level. The ADC is a measure of the diffusivity of water molecules in tissue. In ischemic tissue e.g. following SAH, cytotoxic edema leads to a reduction in the ADC suggesting that the ADC may be a good parameter for identification/quantification of cerebral edema 11 – 13 . Some of the main advantages to using a voxel-by-voxel approach such as VBM are that firstly, it is not biased to one particular structure, and gives a comprehensive assessment of anatomical differences throughout the entire brain without a priori knowledge of which regions may be affected. Furthermore, it is a fully automated process, and therefore is fully reproducible intra- and inter-rater 14 , 15 . For this reason, it is highly suited to the investigation of early brain injury due to the unpredictable nature of the physiological insult that occurs following aneurysm rupture. Furthermore, as early brain injury is characterised by cerebral oedema, using imaging techniques such as ADC and VBM that are sensitive to regional changes in brain tissue is particularly of value. The primary aim of this study was therefore to characterise imaging biomarkers of early brain injury in patients with good clinical grade SAH (WFNS 1 and 2). We aimed to quantify global and regional grey matter volume and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) in patients at three time points: within the first 72 h post-rupture, at 5–10 days and at 3 months post-SAH. We then investigated whether we could predict, within the acute period of the first 72 h post-SAH, the future incidence of cognitive impairment at 3 months post-SAH. Finally, we conducted an exploratory analysis relating our imaging findings with those from the UK Biobank to investigate possible genetic mechanisms underpinning any anatomical differences observed in those with poor cognitive outcome. Our study aimed to build a greater understanding of the pathophysiological changes incurred by aneurysm rupture, and to identify which patients—amongst those initially faring better—were most at risk of poor cognitive outcomes.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Early brain injury after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) within the first 72 hours
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher (up to 80% higher GM volume) compared to controls, including whole-brain GM/WM and regional GM (anterior cingulate/paracingulate gyrus, primary motor cortex, left supramarginal and angular gyrus, fusiform gyrus, basal ganglia, cerebellum).

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Early brain injury after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) within the first 72 hours and at 5-10 days
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lower (up to 100% lower ADC value) in the first 72 hours post-SAH, with a reduction continuing at 5–10 days.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Post-SAH at multiple time points (acute, 5-10 days, 3 months)
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Trend towards higher values at < 72 h, significantly higher at 5–10 days, and a significant increase at 3 months post-SAH compared to healthy controls.

core_effect_and_quantification.biomarker_name: Volume of the posterior cerebellum / Cerebellar GM volume (lobule VII: Crus II, Crus I, VIIb)
core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) and cognitive impairment (acute phase to 3 months post-SAH)
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Widespread apparent higher volume at < 72 h, less marked at 5-10 days, and persistent and significantly higher at 3 months post-SAH in patients, especially those with worse cognitive outcome (Cohen’s d = 0.72). Acute phase normalized GM volume in this region predicted cognitive impairment at 3 months with 84% accuracy, 82% sensitivity, and 86% specificity.

core_effect_and_quantification.biomarker_name: Cognitive impairment (deficits in executive skills, processing speed, non-verbal skills, and memory)
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Almost 50% of patients were defined as cognitively impaired, with significantly worse scores, lower ACE-R scores (89 ± 5 vs 93 ± 5), and a significant decrease in post-SAH IQ (WASI).

core_effect_and_quantification.biomarker_name: Genetic associations (e.g., PAPPA, LRP8, ABCG2, MFHAS1, ZIP8)
core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Associated with Cerebellar GM volume (lobule VII, Crus II) and cardiovascular/stroke-related outcomes
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: PAPPA is a predictor of poor outcome in ischemic stroke. Exonic variants of LRP8 and ABCG2, and intronic variants of MFHAS1 are implicated in familial/premature coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, cardiovascular risk factors, and Type II diabetes. Higher cerebellar GM volume of Crus II is linked to higher risk of cardiovascular death.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Early brain injury, acute stage subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), subsequent post-SAH cognitive impairment, and related cardiovascular disease mechanisms.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: The critical role of the first 72 hours post-aneurysm rupture (early brain injury) in determining clinical and cognitive outcomes after SAH is highlighted. Increased global and regional brain volume and restricted water diffusion (lower ADC) within 72 hours strongly indicate cytotoxic cerebral oedema, where cellular swelling leads to volume increase and decreased water diffusivity. Global cerebral oedema is a significant feature of early brain injury and a risk factor for mortality and poor outcome. Persistent higher grey matter (GM) volume, particularly in cerebellar lobule VII (Crus I, II, and VIIb), is hypothesized to represent residual cerebral oedema or increased injury due to gravity effects and haemotoxicity from high blood load. Damage to the cerebellum, especially lobule VII, is considered critical for higher cognitive functions. This persisting higher cerebellar volume may also serve as a marker for the deleterious influence of proteins relevant to cardiovascular disease, suggesting acute damage to the posterior cerebellum as a potential pathophysiological mechanism for subsequent cognitive impairment.
related_biomarkers: Global and regional grey matter (GM) volume
Posterior cerebellum volume (Crus I, Crus II, VIIb, VIIIa)

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study specifically focused on patients with good clinical grade SAH (WFNS I and II) to identify predictive biomarkers within this subgroup. It suggests that a high blood load (modified Fisher grade 4 and 5) in these good grade SAH patients might lead to increased cerebellar injury due to gravity and haemotoxicity. Higher cerebellar GM volume (lobule VII and VIIIa) was consistently associated with poorer cognitive outcomes.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Cognitive impairment was specifically characterized by deficits in executive skills, processing speed, and non-verbal skills. Regional GM abnormalities were specifically localized bilaterally in the cognitive cerebellar lobule VII (Crus II, Crus I, VIIb) and VIIIa. Acute MRI changes in the posterior cerebellum were able to predict, with an accuracy of 84% (sensitivity 82%, specificity 86%), which good clinical grade SAH patients would develop cognitive impairment 3 months later, despite initially appearing clinically indistinguishable. The voxel-by-voxel approach demonstrated high sensitivity to both global and regional, localized changes. Patients with future impairment paradoxically presented with lower WFNS scores (better clinical condition) upon admission, indicating predictive specificity beyond initial clinical severity.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Patients with good clinical grade aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (WFNS 1 and 2), including those developing cognitive impairment post-SAH. The study also included age/gender-paired healthy controls for comparison and leveraged data from approximately 40,000 UK Biobank participants for genetic analyses.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: The study enables the prediction of future cognitive impairment (deficits in executive skills, processing speed, non-verbal skills, lower ACE-R scores, decreased IQ) at 3 months post-SAH, even in patients initially presenting with a good clinical grade. The presence of higher cerebellar GM volume early after SAH serves as a predictive marker. Global cerebral oedema after SAH is associated with worse initial clinical condition and early brain metabolic distress. Furthermore, genetic associations with cerebellar GM volume suggest links to a higher risk of cardiovascular death, cardiovascular disease, transient ischemic attack, ischemic stroke, familial and premature coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, and Type II diabetes.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The identified acute cerebellar GM volume changes serve as a promising diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for risk stratification. It accurately predicts which good grade SAH patients are at risk of developing poor neurocognitive outcomes despite initial good clinical presentation. The genetic findings further indicate potential risk factors for related health conditions, offering broader diagnostic and prognostic utility.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) and Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) are described as objective, reliable, and non-invasive tools for measuring cerebral structure. VBM is fully automated and reproducible intra- and inter-rater. The normalized GM volume in the cerebellum (scan 3-ROI) measured acutely (scan 1) demonstrated high reliability as a predictive biomarker for cognitive impairment at 3 months post-SAH, achieving a maximum accuracy of 84%, sensitivity of 82%, specificity of 86%, and an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.805 (95% CI: 0.576 to 0.921). The associations between cerebellar GM volume and multiple genes involved in cardiovascular events, as observed in large cohorts like the UK Biobank, further support its relevance and reliability. Routine clinical neuroimaging like CT is noted as less objective for quantifying oedema.
recommended_alternatives: Further investigation will be required to confirm the causality of the identified biomarker (acute cerebellar changes) and its link to cognitive impairment.
Exploration of possible genetic mechanisms underpinning observed anatomical differences, particularly relating imaging findings with UK Biobank data.
